setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. A {client} comes to you for help with {deliverable|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are helping a {client} who has a question about {deliverable|the}.
pressure: Two more {client.plural} are waiting behind this one.
{coworker3} says you are taking too long with each person.
detail: It is the busiest hour of the day.

tiers.1: Keeping the {client} safe comes before the request.
tiers.2: A frustrated {client} needs to feel heard before anything else lands.
tiers.3: You can only promise what the policy and your authority allow.
tiers.4: Give accurate answers, even if that means checking first.
tiers.5: Pointing out a needed item helps the {client} more than a feedback question does.
tiers.6: Inviting feedback is welcome once the request is handled.

fact: You notice {hazard} right where the {client} is standing.
issues.action: Guide the {client} away from the hazard, then make sure it gets marked and reported.
issues.brief: move the {client} away and report the hazard
issues.reason: Service starts with the {client}'s safety. Moving them away prevents an injury, and reporting gets the hazard fixed.
issues.lesson: Protect the people you serve from hazards before handling their request.

shortcut.text: Help the {client} quickly so they can move on before anything happens.
shortcut.brief: help quickly and hope nothing happens
shortcut.why: Hurrying does not remove the hazard. The {client} could be hurt while you help.
shortcut.mis: Fast service makes a hazard less dangerous.

fact: The {client} is frustrated after waiting twenty minutes.
issues.action: Apologize for the wait and acknowledge the frustration before you start helping.
issues.reason: A frustrated person listens better once they feel heard. A sincere apology sets up the rest of the conversation.
issues.lesson: Acknowledge a customer's frustration before solving the problem.

shortcut.text: Explain that the wait was not your fault and get straight to business.
shortcut.brief: say it was not your fault
shortcut.why: Deflecting blame makes the {client} feel dismissed, even if it is true.
shortcut.mis: Explaining whose fault it was calms people down.

fact: The {client} wants a refund, and the posted policy says refunds over $50 need approval from {lead|the}.
clear: {Lead|the} already approved this refund by phone.
issues.action: Explain the policy politely and ask {lead|the} to approve the refund.
issues.reason: The policy sets who can approve larger refunds. Following it, politely, is fair to everyone.
issues.lesson: Serve customers within the limits of your authority, and explain those limits politely.

shortcut.text: Give the refund yourself, since the {client} is a regular.
shortcut.why: The policy requires approval for refunds over $50, whoever the {client} is.
shortcut.mis: Good customers can be treated as exceptions to policy.

fact: The {client} asks a detailed question about {deliverable|the} that you cannot answer.
clear: {coworker} already gave you the answer to the {client}'s question.
issues.done: you already have the answer from {coworker}
issues.action: Say you will find out, and check with {coworker}, who knows the answer.
issues.reason: A wrong answer can cost the {client} time and money. Saying you will check is honest and professional.
issues.lesson: When you do not know, find out rather than guess.

shortcut.text: Give your best guess so the {client} is not kept waiting.
shortcut.why: A guess that turns out wrong damages trust more than a short wait.
shortcut.mis: Any answer is better than saying you need to check.

fact: From the request, you can tell the {client} will also need {supply.plural} to use it.
issues.action: Handle the request, and mention that they will likely need {supply.plural} too.
issues.reason: Pointing out a need before the {client} discovers it later saves them a second trip.
issues.lesson: Anticipate what customers will need next and tell them.

shortcut.text: Say nothing, since the {client} did not ask about {supply.plural}.
shortcut.why: The {client} will likely have to come back. A quick mention prevents that.
shortcut.mis: Good service means answering only what was asked.

fact: The {client} asks how to give feedback about the visit.
issues.action: Tell the {client} how to leave feedback, and thank them for asking.
issues.reason: Feedback helps the workplace improve. Making it easy shows you value the {client}'s view.
issues.lesson: Welcome customer feedback and make it easy to give.

shortcut.text: Say feedback is not really necessary.
shortcut.why: Brushing off feedback suggests the {client}'s view does not matter.

proceed.text: Help the {client} with the request promptly and politely.
proceed.why: Nothing else needs handling first, so prompt, courteous help is exactly what the {client} needs.
proceed.lesson: Courteous, prompt help is the core of good service.

generic.text: Send the {client} to another location that might be less busy.
generic.why: Sending a {client} away without trying to help is poor service.
generic.mis: Passing someone along is the same as helping them.

generic.text: Help the {client} while texting a friend under the counter.
generic.why: Divided attention feels disrespectful and leads to mistakes.
generic.mis: Customers do not notice when you are distracted.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to come and handle the {client} personally.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation is beyond your role. Calling the lead in delays service.
overcaution.mis: A supervisor always gives better service.

upset: The {client} has been waiting a long time and is frustrated.
refund: The {client} is asking for a refund that is larger than you can approve.
unknown: The {client} has a question you cannot answer yourself.

steps.text: Greet the {client} by making eye contact
Complete the request and confirm it is right

rel: The apology comes as part of the greeting.
Acknowledge the wait before asking them to explain.
Greet before getting into the request.
You need the details before asking for approval.
You need to know the question before checking the answer.
The refund can only be completed once approved.
You complete the request with the right answer.
You resolve the request after hearing it.
process.lesson: Greet, acknowledge, listen, get what you need, then resolve and confirm.

review.notes: Refund limit stated as a posted policy. Refund and unknown-answer are exclusive because either order is reasonable.

kits.familyName: Following through on a promised callback
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. This morning you promised a {client} a call back by 3 p.m. about a problem with {deliverable|the}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you told a {client} you would call back by 3 p.m. with an answer about {deliverable|the}.
pressure: {coworker3} says {client.plural} never notice if a callback is a little late.
detail: You wrote the promise on a sticky note.

tiers.1: Account details are shared only after identity is confirmed.
tiers.2: A promise you cannot keep should be updated before it is broken.
tiers.3: Getting the {client} to the right team beats a slow answer from the wrong one.
tiers.4: Coworkers who serve the {client} deserve the same prompt help.
tiers.5: Following up on a fix is valuable once nothing is pending.

fact: The person who answers asks about the account but has not confirmed their identity, which the posted policy requires.
clear: The person on the phone already confirmed their identity using the security questions.
issues.done: the caller's identity was already confirmed
issues.action: Confirm the person's identity, as the policy requires, before sharing any details.
issues.reason: The policy protects the {client}'s information. Confirming identity first keeps it from reaching the wrong person.
issues.lesson: Follow identity checks before sharing account information, even when you are in a hurry.

shortcut.text: Share the details, since the person sounds like the {client}.
shortcut.brief: share details because they sound right
shortcut.why: Sounding familiar is not confirmation. The policy exists to protect the {client}.
shortcut.mis: You can tell who someone is by their voice.

fact: You will not have the answer by 3 p.m. as you promised.
issues.short: the callback promise you cannot keep
issues.action: Call the {client} before 3 p.m. to explain and give a new time.
issues.brief: call before 3 to give a new time
issues.reason: A quick update keeps your word in spirit and shows the {client} you have not forgotten them.
issues.lesson: If you cannot keep a promise, update the customer before the deadline passes.

shortcut.text: Wait until you have the answer, even if that means calling tomorrow.
shortcut.brief: wait until you have the answer
shortcut.why: Silence after a promised call feels like being ignored. A short update prevents that.
shortcut.mis: Calling without an answer is pointless.

fact: You learn that the question really belongs to the billing team, not yours.
issues.action: Connect the {client} with billing and pass along what they already told you.
issues.brief: connect them to billing with the details
issues.reason: Passing along the details means the {client} does not have to explain everything again.
issues.lesson: When handing a customer to another team, pass along what you know.

shortcut.text: Give the {client} the billing number and let them start over.
shortcut.why: Making the {client} repeat everything is frustrating and wastes their time.
shortcut.mis: Giving a phone number is the same as a handoff.

fact: {coworker} in billing asks you for the order details so they can help the {client}.
issues.action: Send {coworker} the order details promptly, as you would for any {client}.
issues.reason: Coworkers who depend on you are internal customers. Helping them quickly helps the {client} too.
issues.lesson: Treat coworkers who need your help as customers too.

shortcut.text: Tell {coworker} you will get to it after your own callbacks.
shortcut.why: Delaying the details delays the {client}'s answer.
shortcut.mis: Internal requests matter less than external ones.

clear: You already sent {coworker} the order details this morning.
issues.done: the details were already sent to {coworker}

fact: The problem was fixed yesterday, but nobody has checked whether the {client} is happy with the result.
issues.action: Ask the {client} whether the fix worked and whether anything else is needed.
issues.reason: A short follow-up confirms the problem is really solved and shows you care about the result.
issues.lesson: Follow up to make sure a fix actually worked for the customer.

shortcut.text: Assume the {client} is happy, since nobody has complained.
shortcut.why: Silence does not mean satisfaction. A short check catches problems early.
shortcut.mis: No complaint means a happy customer.

proceed.text: Call the {client} back at the promised time with the answer.
proceed.why: You have the answer and nothing else needs handling, so keeping the promise is the right move.
proceed.lesson: Keep your service promises on time.

generic.text: Email the {client} a long explanation instead of calling as promised.
generic.why: You promised a call. Changing the format without asking can feel like avoidance.
generic.mis: Any form of contact keeps the promise.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to make the call so you can leave early.
generic.why: The promise was yours. Handing it off to leave early is unreliable service.
generic.mis: Anyone can keep a promise you made.

overcaution.text: Check with {lead|the} before making the call.
overcaution.why: You have everything needed. Checking with the lead first could make you late.
overcaution.mis: Every customer call needs supervisor approval.

title: Your follow-up email to the {client}
intro: You are about to email the {client} after this morning's call. Check the message first.
doc.lesson: Service messages should be courteous, accurate and clear about what happens next.

lines.text: Thank you for your patience while we looked into the problem.
Our billing team has the details you gave me, so you will not need to repeat them.

bad.text: Please call billing and explain the whole problem to them from the beginning.
bad.why: Making the {client} repeat everything is frustrating. The details should be passed along.

lines.text: You can expect a call from {coworker} in billing by noon tomorrow.
lines.fine: Gives a specific next step and time.

bad.text: Someone will probably get back to you at some point.
bad.why: A vague promise leaves the {client} unsure what happens next.

lines.text: If you have questions before then, reply to this email.
lines.fine: Offers a way to follow up.

bad.text: Please do not reply to this email.
bad.why: Cutting off replies leaves the {client} no way to ask questions.

lines.text: We are sorry for the trouble this caused.

bad.text: This would have been simpler if you had read the instructions.
bad.why: Blaming the {client} is discourteous and damages the relationship.

lines.text: For your security, we will not include account numbers in email.

bad.text: Your full account number and security answers are listed below for reference.
bad.why: Sending account numbers and security answers by email puts the {client}'s information at risk.

review.notes: Identity check stated as posted policy.
